strengths: DDOME addresses a useful problem: selecting a small expert subset for previously unseen federated clients using unlabeled local inputs, without test-time fine-tuning. The explicit losses and pseudocode make the proposed mechanism understandable.

The reported results suggest practical promise across four classification datasets. Improvements over the common expert itself, including 78.6% versus 73% on CIFAR100 and 74.9% versus 69% on Yahoo! Answers, indicate potential benefits beyond simply retaining the pretrained model.

The appendices provide useful experiments on anchor ratios, representation quality, overlapping anchor distributions, matched expert counts, and changing client populations. These help identify conditions under which the method succeeds.
The limitations candidly acknowledge dependence on pretrained representations, communication overhead, restricted scalability testing, and potential fairness risks.
weaknesses: Theorem 1's constant loss lower bound is invalid as stated. Choose m=2, ground-truth routing vectors e_1 and e_2, and expert vectors e_3 and e_4. Under the stated covariance I_d/√d, the zero predictor has loss 1/(2√d). Both exact optimization stages can only reduce this loss, contradicting the claimed Ω(1) lower bound. Appendix J also changes the covariance to I_d/d and omits covariance factors in subsequent calculations. Independently, the projection bound on page 25 fails when W*=V*, an allowed case, because the projected subspace contains V*. These require substantive theoretical corrections.

The claimed necessity of joint training exceeds the scope of the analyzed procedure. Even a corrected result would concern experts trained under a random fixed router followed by router optimization with frozen experts, under linear Gaussian assumptions. It would not establish necessity across other staged training procedures or explain DDOME's anchored federated optimization. Direct joint-versus-staged training ablations are missing.

The main experiments supply substantial specialization structure through anchor construction: anchors receive disjoint label groups, fixed expert assignments, supervised routing targets, and frequent activation. Consequently, the results do not isolate discovery from implicit heterogeneity alone. The overlapping-anchor experiment is helpful, but automatic anchor selection and controls separating label-informed bootstrapping from learned specialization remain necessary. Generalization evidence is confined to new mixtures of known labels.

The comparisons do not adequately substantiate state-of-the-art claims. Main experiments use 5–10 experts for DDOME versus two for FedMix, and several baselines deteriorate dramatically from strong initial checkpoints—for example, CIFAR10 FedAvg falls from 93% to 58.4%. Text optimization schedules also differ across methods. Appendix G partially addresses expert-count matching, but transparently tuned comparisons under matched capacity and resource budgets remain needed. Appendix I's k-means illustration does not replace quantitative comparisons with relevant clustered or personalized federated methods.

Reproducibility is incomplete where it matters most. The common-expert checkpoints' training data and preparation procedure are insufficiently specified despite their decisive effect on performance. Router dimensions, the text learning-rate decay factor, partition seeds, and experimental repetition counts are also missing. Main tables lack uncertainty estimates, and reporting best test accuracies in several appendix tables without a specified validation protocol weakens confidence in robustness.

The efficiency contribution is insufficiently measured. Transmitting K rather than M experts establishes a structural communication saving, but the paper does not report comparable transmitted bytes, inference latency, or full encoder costs. Overall efficiency relative to the main single-model and two-expert baselines therefore remains unclear.
